problem.title: Retail demand forecasting
problem.context: A retailer forecasts weekly demand per store and product for 400 stores and 30,000 products. Every Monday forecasts for the next eight weeks feed replenishment. Nightly till sales arrive in the data warehouse; promotions and public holidays strongly affect demand. Three data scientists own the pipeline, and central IT runs a warehouse they cannot change.

requirements.text: Produce, every week, the forecast per store and product for the next eight weeks, and deliver it to the replenishment system by Monday 06:00.
Run the forecast again for any past week exactly as it was produced.
Try new model ideas and compare them with the production model on past weeks before they replace it.
Asked for the forecast of a week up to two years back, the team produces the same numbers within one working day.
A new model idea that beats the production model on past weeks reaches production within one week, with no manual step except the approval.
When a weekly run fails, the team is told within 15 minutes, and the replenishment system never receives a partial forecast.
A new team member can run the whole pipeline on their own machine within their first week.
Three data scientists, with no data engineers; the data warehouse stays as it is.
The weekly run must fit in the six hours between the nightly load and the Monday deadline.

approaches.idea: What if a managed container batch job provides the simplest repeatable end-to-end pipeline?
What if the warehouse performs the forecasting and delivery close to the source data?
approaches.dropped_because: It depends on warehouse-side compute and direct mutable delivery that the data-science team cannot change or safely operate, conflicting with C1 and Q3.

approaches.idea: What if a small scheduled VM keeps the runtime familiar and under the team's direct control?
What if a managed workflow engine coordinates ephemeral compute for resilient runs?
What if a lightweight scheduled container job makes each run a portable, self-describing package?

values: Execution: Managed container batch
History: Immutable weekly input snapshots
Promotion: Git champion challenger with approval
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Managed batch and frozen inputs should meet R1, R2, Q1, Q3, and C1 with little platform work; a Git-based challenger path should support R3 and Q2, subject to workflow automation maturity.
trajectory.observation: The combination is operationally small and replayable. The six-hour window needs a measured run, and a Git workflow may still leave repeatable evaluation or packaging steps manual.

values: Execution: Warehouse-native SQL
History: Re-query warehouse with versioned SQL
Promotion: Manual model file replacement
Delivery: Direct table overwrite
Operations: Existing scheduler alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Keeping compute near warehouse data may help R1 and C2, but re-querying mutable history and direct writes risk R2, Q1, Q2, and Q3; warehouse changes may violate C1.
trajectory.observation: Warehouse-side changes are outside the team's control, and direct overwrites cannot protect replenishment from partial results. This approach fails the no-change constraint and reliability requirement.

values: Execution: Single scheduled VM
History: Immutable weekly input snapshots
Promotion: Git champion challenger with approval
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Host and run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: A familiar, compact runtime should meet C1 and Q4, while snapshots and atomic publication support replay and Q3; host capacity and manual model packaging may limit C2 and Q2.
trajectory.observation: A VM is easy to understand and run locally, but the six-hour capacity and timely host alerting require active ownership. Promotion remains less automatic than the requirements ask.

values: Execution: Managed workflow with ephemeral workers
History: Immutable weekly input snapshots
Promotion: Model registry promotion with approval
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Managed orchestration, workers, and registry should make retries, alerts, and challenger review robust for R1-R3 and Q1-Q3; added platform concepts may burden C1 and Q4.
trajectory.observation: The managed services cover operational needs, but the registry's integration and the additional workflow concepts increase what three scientists must learn and maintain. Registry promotion also needs an automated approval path.

values: Execution: Managed container batch
History: Immutable weekly input snapshots
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Replacing the loosely defined Git process with CI evaluation and a tagged artifact should improve Q2 while preserving the batch design's strengths; C2 still needs a measured capacity run.
trajectory.observation: CI can run the same historical comparisons and produce the promoted artifact after approval, removing manual packaging. Runtime remains a workload benchmark rather than a guaranteed property.

values: Execution: Single scheduled VM
History: Snapshot extracts with code and model manifest
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Recording inputs, code, and model together should strengthen exact replay, and CI plus managed alerts should improve Q1-Q3 without adding a complex runtime.
trajectory.observation: The self-contained run record and automation resolve the original process gaps while keeping the VM model approachable. The team still owns capacity and host maintenance, and six-hour fit needs a benchmark.

values: Execution: Managed workflow with ephemeral workers
History: Immutable weekly input snapshots
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Using standard CI approval and tagged artifacts instead of a specialized registry workflow should improve Q2 and reduce the maintenance burden on the small team.
trajectory.observation: The CI path simplifies model promotion, while the workflow engine still adds concepts and integration work. The design remains viable if the selected managed platform is already familiar to the team.

values: Execution: Managed container job with lightweight scheduler
History: Snapshot extracts with code and model manifest
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: A lightweight scheduler around a self-describing container should retain managed alerting and automated promotion while reducing orchestration overhead; snapshots plus code and model manifests should make R2 and Q1 concrete.
trajectory.observation: This combines the portable runtime with a durable replay record and automated promotion, avoiding both a broad workflow stack and persistent host administration. Capacity still needs measurement.

values: Execution: Managed container batch
History: Snapshot extracts with code and model manifest
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Bind the managed batch's frozen data to explicit code and model manifests to test whether the run record makes historical reconstruction more dependable; C2 still needs a benchmark.
trajectory.observation: The stronger run manifest makes the replay boundary explicit without changing the operationally simple batch design. A measured forecast run is still needed to establish six-hour fit.

values: Execution: Single scheduled VM
History: Immutable weekly input snapshots
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact
Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Use immutable weekly snapshots with the automated VM release path to test whether the simpler retention model remains sufficient for replay and Q1.
trajectory.observation: Immutable snapshots retain exact historical data while avoiding a manifest convention beyond the normal code and model version record. Host upkeep and capacity remain team responsibilities.

values: Execution: Managed workflow with ephemeral workers
History: Snapshot extracts with code and model manifest
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact

Operations: Managed run alerts
trajectory.hypothesis: Add an explicit code and model manifest to managed workflow snapshots so an orchestrated run remains self-describing during replay.
trajectory.observation: The explicit run record strengthens replay in a complex orchestration path, but it does not remove the learning and maintenance burden for the small team.

values: Execution: Managed container job with lightweight scheduler

Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact

trajectory.hypothesis: Retain immutable weekly snapshots in the lightweight packaged-job design to test whether fewer run-record conventions keep the leanest option maintainable while preserving replay.
trajectory.observation: The packaged job remains portable and replayable with a simpler input archive; the only unresolved requirement is measured fit in the six-hour window.

adrs.title: Choose the weekly execution environment
adrs.context: The pipeline must produce about 96 million store-product-horizon values each week inside a six-hour window. Three data scientists need a runtime they can operate and reproduce locally, and the warehouse cannot be changed. Managed execution reduces host work, while a small VM can be easier to understand; either path needs a real workload benchmark.

options.name: Managed container batch
values: Execution: Managed container batch
pros: No persistent host for the team to administer.
A container gives a consistent execution environment.
cons: Capacity and service limits need validation against the six-hour window.
options.reason: Choose for a straightforward managed batch lifecycle with low operational overhead.

options.name: Single scheduled VM
values: Execution: Single scheduled VM
pros: Simple runtime model and easy local reproduction.
Direct control over installed libraries and compute.
cons: The team owns host maintenance and capacity planning.
options.reason: Choose when the workload fits one machine and the team values a familiar runtime.

options.name: Managed workflow with ephemeral workers
values: Execution: Managed workflow with ephemeral workers
pros: Managed orchestration supports retries and elastic workers.
cons: More platform concepts and integrations for a three-person team.
options.reason: Choose when workflow recovery and scaling justify the added operational model.

options.name: Lightweight scheduled container job
values: Execution: Managed container job with lightweight scheduler
pros: Portable packaged runtime with a small orchestration surface.
cons: The lightweight scheduler offers fewer workflow features than a dedicated engine.
options.reason: Choose for a compact managed design that keeps the run model easy to understand.

options.name: Warehouse-native SQL
values: Execution: Warehouse-native SQL
pros: Could place calculations near the existing sales data.
cons: Requires warehouse-side compute changes and direct writes that the team cannot safely control.
options.reason: Discard because it conflicts with C1 and cannot ensure atomic delivery.

adrs.title: Preserve forecast inputs and automate model promotion
adrs.context: Historical forecasts need to be reconstructed exactly, and a challenger that wins should reach production after approval without manual packaging. Re-querying a changing warehouse is not enough for exact replay. Freezing inputs and binding them to versioned code and model artifacts improves reproducibility, with storage and CI work as the cost.

options.name: Immutable snapshots and Git comparison
values: History: Immutable weekly input snapshots
Promotion: Git champion challenger with approval
pros: Frozen data makes historical replay dependable.
Git provides a familiar model history.
cons: The release process may still require manual evaluation or packaging.
options.reason: Retained as a seed but superseded by an explicit CI artifact path for Q2.

options.name: Immutable snapshots and CI artifacts
values: History: Immutable weekly input snapshots
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact
pros: CI can repeat challenger comparisons and create a tagged release after approval.
cons: Snapshot retention and CI workflows need ownership.
options.reason: Choose for reliable replay with a compact snapshot record and an approval-only promotion path.

options.name: Run manifest and CI artifacts
values: History: Snapshot extracts with code and model manifest
Promotion: CI approval and tagged model artifact
pros: Binds data, code, and model versions for a specific run.
cons: Run manifests and snapshot storage need disciplined retention.
options.reason: Choose when a self-describing run record best supports portability and replay.

options.name: Re-query warehouse and manual replacement
values: History: Re-query warehouse with versioned SQL
Promotion: Manual model file replacement
cons: Changing warehouse contents can alter replay, and replacement steps are manual.
options.reason: Discard because it misses reproducibility and development velocity.

adrs.title: Make delivery complete and failures visible
adrs.context: Replenishment must receive a full weekly forecast by Monday 06:00, and failures must be reported within 15 minutes. Writing directly into the live destination risks exposing partial output. Staging plus an atomic manifest or pointer switch delays visibility until the complete forecast is ready; managed run alerts reduce custom operations.

options.name: Stage, atomically publish, and alert
values: Delivery: Staged output and atomic manifest publish
Operations: Managed run alerts
pros: Failed runs leave the previous complete forecast visible.
Managed alerts notify the team without custom monitoring infrastructure.
cons: The consumer must read through the manifest or equivalent atomic switch.
options.reason: Choose to protect the replenishment handoff and give prompt failure visibility.

options.name: Direct overwrite with existing alerts
values: Delivery: Direct table overwrite
Operations: Existing scheduler alerts
pros: Simple destination flow with little extra staging.
cons: Partial writes may be visible and existing alert timing is not assured.
options.reason: Discard because it cannot guarantee complete publication or the 15-minute alert target.
